nameStory: Peck's Skipper honors William Dandridge Peck, one of America's first entomologists who taught at Harvard University in the early 1800s. Professor Peck was passionate about documenting New England's insects, so it's fitting that this common regional butterfly bears his name. Like many scientific names from that era, it celebrates the pioneering naturalists who first studied our local wildlife.
description: Peck's Skipper is a small, golden-brown butterfly that belongs to the skipper family - butterflies known for their quick, darting flight patterns that seem to 'skip' through the air. Adults have a wingspan of about 1 to 1.5 inches, with tawny orange wings marked by distinctive dark borders and spots. The males are typically brighter orange than the females, and both sexes have a stocky body typical of skippers. You'll often see them perched with their wings held at different angles - front wings up, back wings horizontal.

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive yellow-orange patches on dark brown wings, with males showing a prominent dark diagonal line (called a stigma) on their forewings that feels slightly raised if you could touch it

idTips.label: Size and Shape
idTips.description: Small butterfly with a wingspan about the size of a half-dollar coin, with triangular forewings and a robust, fuzzy body that looks almost moth-like

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Flies in quick, erratic bursts with rapid wingbeats, then glides briefly - like watching someone skip stones across water

idTips.label: Perching Behavior
idTips.description: Often sits with wings partially open at different angles rather than fully spread flat, and tends to perch low on flowers or grass stems

idTips.label: Antennae Shape
idTips.description: Club-tipped antennae that curve backward into a small hook at the end, distinguishing them from moths which have feathery or straight antennae

habitat: Peck's Skipper thrives in open, sunny areas with plenty of grasses, including meadows, fields, roadsides, and suburban lawns throughout New England. They're particularly fond of areas where native grasses grow alongside wildflowers like clover, asters, and black-eyed susans. You'll often find them in slightly disturbed habitats like old pastures, park edges, and even well-maintained gardens with mixed plantings.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late May, with fresh individuals showing bright, unmarked wings. Look for mating behaviors and females laying eggs on grass blades.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity from June through August, with multiple generations producing a steady stream of butterflies. Adults are most active on warm, sunny days visiting flowers for nectar.
seasonality.fall: Last generation flies into early September, with individuals often showing worn, faded wings from summer activity. Adults focus on building fat reserves before winter.
seasonality.winter: Overwinters as caterpillars in grass tussocks, completely hidden from view. No adult activity during this season in New England.

funFact: Peck's Skipper caterpillars are master architects that create silk-lined tubes within grass clumps, essentially building tiny underground apartments where they live and feed throughout winter - some entomologists call these structures 'grass condos' because multiple caterpillars may share the same grass clump!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Tawny-edged Skipper, which is slightly smaller and has more muted orange coloring. Remember: Peck's has PROminent patches (Peck's = Prominent), while Tawny-edged looks more evenly colored overall. The Northern Broken-Dash has distinctive white spots on the underwing that Peck's lacks.
contextualKnowledge: Skippers are sometimes called 'the third group' of Lepidoptera because they share characteristics of both butterflies and moths - they hold their wings like butterflies but have thick, fuzzy bodies like moths. This can confuse beginners who expect all butterflies to look delicate and graceful.
compareHints: Compared to its genus relatives, Peck's Skipper shows the brightest and most contrasting orange patches - Northern Broken-Dash appears more subdued with prominent white underwing spots, while Tawny-edged Skipper has a more uniform tawny color without Peck's bold orange patches. Peck's males also have the most prominent dark stigma line of the three species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to Peck's Skipper, the Northern Broken-Dash lacks the bright orange patches and has a more subdued brown coloration overall.

Among its Polites cousins, the tawny-edged skipper is distinguished from Peck's skipper by lacking the clear white hindwing spots, and from the northern broken-dash by having continuous golden edges rather than broken or interrupted markings.
